story: The Burmese has a heavy heart and a velvet coat. Pick one up and you notice the weight first. Fans say it is a brick wrapped in silk.

Nearly every Burmese traces to one cat. In 1930 Dr. Joseph Thompson of San Francisco brought home a small brown female named Wong Mau after a trip to Burma. He bred her to Siamese cats, and sable kittens without pointed markings started the breed.
Wong Mau turned out to be a cross between a Siamese and a Burmese type. That is why her line also gave the world the Tonkinese.
The Cat Fanciers' Association registered the Burmese in 1936. It later paused recognition while breeders argued over outcrossing, and restored it for good in 1954.
Two types exist today. The American Burmese is stocky with a round face. The European type is longer and finer.

Burmese are people cats. They are playful, attentive, and chatty like their Siamese ancestors, but with softer voices. Many learn to fetch. Most will pick your lap, your book, or your journal, and sit right in the middle of it.
fblocks: Named for Burma, now Myanmar, where Wong Mau's journey began. The breed itself was developed in California.
Wong Mau, the brown cat of 1930 who founded the breed. Her line also gave the world the Tonkinese.
Social and chatty, and unhappy alone all day. Often playful into old age. Ask the breeder about genetic testing and diabetes risk.
A short, satin coat that lies close to the body. CFA colors are sable, champagne, blue, and platinum. Yellow eyes.
8 to 12 pounds. About 12 to 16 years. Registered by the CFA in 1936. Ranked 19th of 45 breeds in 2018.
days: Most Burmese cats trace back to one brown cat named Wong Mau.
Dr. Joseph Thompson carried Wong Mau from Burma to San Francisco in 1930.
Burmese weigh more than they look. Fans call them bricks wrapped in silk.
Your journal is now a cat bed. Write around the cat.
A warm mug, a cold window, and one good view. That is enough.
A Burmese talks like a Siamese, only softer. Ask your friends.
A quilt, a fire, and a Burmese asleep on your side of the bed.
last_walk:
The lamp is on, and the snow keeps falling.
The Burmese has followed you from room to room all week. It has sat on your book, your sweater, and your plans. Now it curls into the quilt with a sigh, content to be exactly where you are. A heavy little heart, warm all the way through.
